newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels exaggerate progress in Shaba - sources.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels exaggerate progress in Shaba - sources.

text.p: Rebel claims to be on the brink of capturing Zaire's copper capital are exaggerated, expatriate sources said on Thursday.
Government officials and the expatriates in Lubumbashi, capital of Shaba province, said the town of Kasenga, 200 km (125 miles) to the north, was still held by Zairean troops.
On Wednesday the rebel radio, Voice of the People, said Laurent Kabila's forces were within 100 km (60 miles) of Lubumbashi, Zaire's copper capital and second biggest city.
The expatriate sources, who declined to be further identified, were in contact with Kasenga and doubted the rebels had skirted the town on the Zambian border.
The rebels have captured about a quarter of Africa's third largest country since the revolt against President Mobutu Sese Seko began last October.

Shaba, its soil stuffed with copper, cobalt and precious metals, would be a fabulous prize for the rebels. Despite agreeing on Thursday to talks with the Mobutu regime in the next few days, the rebels have not announced a ceasefire.
Mobutu's army has collapsed against the rebels so far. The recruitment of about 300 mainly Serbian mercenaries failed to prevent the loss earlier in March of the key city of Kisangani.

Government troops were also in control at Minga, half way between Kasenga and Lubumbashi, after some trouble on Wednesday in which two people were killed, according to truck drivers who passed through the town.

"We first saw burning houses as we approached from Kasenga. Minga was deserted, apart from goats and soldiers. There were about 50 soldiers, guns at the ready," said Herve, a driver whom the army allowed to pass through to Lubumbashi.
He and other drivers said they had seen two or three bodies, dressed in civilian clothes, lying by the roadside.

The expatriate sources said they did not believe rebel troops had penetrated so far south, but that people in outlying parts of Shaba, eagerly awaiting the arrival of Kabila's disciplined fighters, had taken to openly showing their support.
"If there was a clash it could have been with them, or with other loose-cannon Zairean soldiers retreating from the front lines further north," said one source.
